intro: How long is your desk? What time is lunch? How much is in your pocket? Every day you measure things. This unit shows you how. You will lay units end to end. You will read a ruler in inches and centimeters. You will make a graph of what you find.

Then you will learn the clock. The short hand tells the hour. The long hand counts minutes by fives. You will know when it is 3:00 and when it is 3:30. You will know the difference between a.m. and p.m.
Last, you will count coins. Pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters each have a value. You will add them up, buy things and give change. By the end, you can run a bake sale table all by yourself.
bigQuestion: How do we use numbers to say how long, what time and how much?

timeline.t: Wake up. The short hand is on the 7, the long hand on the 12.
School starts. The long hand points to the 6: half past 8.
Measure the hallway in shoes, then in feet with a tape.
Make a bar graph of everyone's shoe lengths.
Lunch. The clock hands both point straight up.
Sort the bake sale coins: quarters, dimes, nickels, pennies.
Count the coins. Big coins first: 25, 35, 45, 50.
A cookie costs 35¢. Count up to make change from 50¢.
The bell rings. School is over for the day.
Dinner. Tell someone at home what time it is.

words.d: the one thing you use over and over to measure, like a cube or an inch
a small unit of length; a paper clip is about 1 inch
a unit of length equal to 12 inches
a small unit of length, about the width of a pinky finger; 100 make a meter
a graph with bars; a taller bar means a bigger count
the short hand on a clock; it points to the hour
the smallest amount of U.S. money; a penny is one cent
the money you get back when you pay more than the price

test.q: Two sticks start at the same line. The blue stick sticks out past the other one. Which is longer?
test.why: With the ends lined up, the stick that reaches farther is longer. That is the blue one.

test.q: You measure a table with cubes. The cubes overlap. What happens to your count?
test.why: Overlapping cubes each cover less new space. More cubes fit, so the count is too big.

test.q: How many inches are in one foot?
test.why: One foot is 12 inches. A 12-inch ruler is one foot long.

test.q: How many centimeters are in one meter?
A picture graph shows 5 apples and 3 bananas. How many more apples than bananas?
test.why: 5 − 3 = 2 more apples. Adding gives 8, which is the total.

test.q: The short hand is between 2 and 3. The long hand is on the 6. What time is it?
test.why: Long hand on 6 means half past. The short hand passed the 2, so it is 2:30.

test.q: The long hand points to the 10. How many minutes past the hour is it?
test.why: Count by fives to the 10: 10 fives is 50. It is 50 minutes past.

test.q: One quarter and two dimes. How many cents?
A pencil costs 30¢. A pen costs 45¢. How much for both?
A snack costs 65¢. You pay with three quarters, 75¢. How much change do you get?
test.why: Count up from 65 to 75. That is 10. Check: 75 − 65 = 10.

write.prompt: You have one quarter, two dimes and one nickel. You buy a cookie for 35¢. How much money do you have? How much is left after you buy the cookie? Explain each step.
tips: Count the coins big to small: 25, 35, 45, 50.
Check by counting up from 35 to 50.
Say why your answer makes sense.
